questions.question: A startup's monolithic application handles 1,000 requests/second on a single server. Traffic is expected to grow 10x in 6 months. The team debates between upgrading to a more powerful server vs. adding more servers. Which factors favor horizontal scaling in this scenario? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: The application is stateless and can run on multiple instances
The team wants to avoid single points of failure
The database is the primary bottleneck
Cost-effectiveness at higher scale

questions.explanation: Horizontal scaling works well for stateless apps, eliminates SPOF, and is often more cost-effective at scale. If the database is the bottleneck, adding app servers won't help—you'd need to scale the database layer separately. This is why companies like Netflix moved from vertical scaling to horizontal scaling with microservices—they needed both fault tolerance and cost efficiency at massive scale. The key insight is that horizontal scaling addresses application-tier bottlenecks, not data-tier bottlenecks.

questions.question: An e-commerce platform experiences 50x traffic spikes during flash sales. Which scaling approach allows the system to handle these temporary spikes most cost-effectively?

options.text: Permanently provisioning for peak capacity with reserved instances
Vertical scaling with larger instance types during sales
Horizontal auto-scaling with on-demand instances
Pre-warming a fixed pool of instances before each sale event

questions.explanation: Auto-scaling horizontally with on-demand instances handles temporary spikes without paying for idle capacity. Amazon's own retail platform uses this approach during Prime Day—scaling from baseline to handle 100x+ traffic spikes, then scaling back down. Permanent provisioning wastes ~98% of resources during normal periods. Vertical scaling requires downtime and has upper limits. Pre-warming helps but still leaves you paying for unused capacity between events. The fundamental principle is matching resource allocation to actual demand curves.

questions.question: A video processing service needs to scale. Each video transcoding job requires 32GB RAM and 8 CPU cores, and jobs cannot be parallelized internally. What is the most appropriate scaling strategy?

options.text: Horizontal scaling with many small instances sharing job fragments
Vertical scaling with progressively larger single instances
Horizontal scaling with appropriately-sized instances for job requirements
Serverless functions with memory allocation matching job needs

questions.explanation: Since individual jobs need significant resources and can't be split, you need instances sized to handle one job (32GB RAM, 8 cores minimum). But to handle multiple concurrent jobs, you scale horizontally with multiple such instances. Pure vertical scaling limits concurrency to one job at a time. Small instances can't run the jobs at all. Serverless functions typically have memory limits (AWS Lambda maxes at 10GB) that won't accommodate 32GB requirements. YouTube's transcoding pipeline uses this exact pattern—appropriately-sized workers that scale horizontally based on queue depth.

questions.question: Which statements about vertical scaling are TRUE? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: It has an upper limit based on available hardware
It typically requires application code changes to utilize additional resources
It can usually be performed with zero downtime on cloud platforms
It maintains a single point of failure

questions.explanation: Vertical scaling is limited by maximum available hardware (AWS's largest instance is ~24TB RAM, 448 vCPUs) and keeps the SPOF. It usually doesn't require code changes—that's actually an advantage, as the same code runs on bigger hardware. However, it typically requires downtime for hardware changes, even on cloud platforms (instance stop/start). This is why Twitter's early 'Fail Whale' era ended when they moved from vertical scaling of Ruby on Rails to horizontal scaling with the JVM—they hit both the hardware ceiling and the SPOF problem simultaneously.

questions.question: A social media app stores user sessions in memory on each application server. The team wants to horizontally scale the app tier. What must they address first?

options.text: Database connection pooling to handle more concurrent connections
Session state management to enable stateless application instances
Load balancer configuration for even traffic distribution
DNS TTL settings for faster failover between instances

questions.explanation: In-memory sessions make the app stateful—users would lose their session if routed to a different server. They must externalize session storage (Redis, Memcached, database) or use sticky sessions before horizontal scaling works correctly. This is the 'Twelve-Factor App' principle of stateless processes. Shopify learned this lesson scaling their Ruby on Rails monolith—they moved sessions to Redis, enabling true horizontal scaling. Connection pooling, load balancer config, and DNS settings are important but secondary to solving the fundamental statefulness problem.

questions.question: A database is the bottleneck in a read-heavy application (95% reads, 5% writes). Which scaling strategies are most effective? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Add read replicas to distribute read load
Implement a caching layer to reduce database hits
Shard the database to distribute data across nodes
Vertically scale the primary database server

questions.explanation: For read-heavy workloads, read replicas and caching directly address the bottleneck by offloading reads from the primary. Facebook's TAO cache handles billions of reads per second, reducing database load by 99%+. Sharding primarily helps write scaling and adds significant complexity for read-heavy workloads. Vertical scaling has limits and doesn't distribute load. The key insight is matching the scaling strategy to the workload pattern—read replicas for read scaling, sharding for write scaling, caching for both but especially reads.

questions.question: An application currently runs on a single 64-core server at 80% CPU utilization. The team is considering scaling options. If they switch to horizontal scaling with 8-core instances, approximately how many instances would they need to handle the same load?

options.text: 6-7 instances (accounting for ~10% overhead)
8 instances (simple core division)
10-12 instances (accounting for coordination overhead)
Cannot be determined without understanding workload characteristics

questions.explanation: CPU cores don't scale linearly across instances due to coordination overhead, network latency, load balancer overhead, memory bandwidth differences, and application-specific factors like lock contention. A CPU-bound single-threaded workload might need only 7 instances, while a coordination-heavy workload might need 15+. Amdahl's Law applies here—the serial portion of your workload limits parallel speedup. LinkedIn discovered this when scaling their feed generation: theoretical calculations suggested 10 instances, but coordination overhead required 18 in practice.

questions.question: Which is a key disadvantage of horizontal scaling compared to vertical scaling?

options.text: Higher per-unit hardware costs at any scale
Increased operational and architectural complexity
Inability to handle stateful workloads
Requirement for specialized distributed databases

questions.explanation: Horizontal scaling introduces complexity: load balancing, distributed state management, network communication, deployment coordination, service discovery, and monitoring across instances. Vertical scaling is operationally simpler—one box to manage. This complexity cost is why startups often begin with vertical scaling and migrate to horizontal only when necessary. Basecamp famously runs on a small number of powerful servers rather than many small ones, accepting the SPOF tradeoff for operational simplicity. The choice depends on your team's capacity to manage distributed systems.

questions.question: A system architect proposes 'scale cube' dimensions for a growing application. Which represents scaling by splitting different functionalities?

options.text: X-axis: horizontal duplication of identical instances
Y-axis: functional decomposition into separate services
Z-axis: data partitioning by customer or attribute
All axes must be applied together for effective scaling

questions.explanation: The AKF Scale Cube defines: X-axis (cloning/horizontal scaling—running multiple identical copies), Y-axis (functional decomposition—splitting into microservices by business capability), Z-axis (data partitioning/sharding—splitting by customer, geography, or data attribute). eBay used all three: X-axis for web servers, Y-axis to split into 200+ services, Z-axis to shard by seller ID. Each axis addresses different scaling challenges and can be applied independently or together based on bottlenecks.

questions.question: A startup claims horizontal scaling is always more cost-effective than vertical scaling. Under what conditions is this claim FALSE?

options.text: When the application requires specialized hardware accelerators
When operational complexity costs exceed hardware savings
When the workload is small enough that one server suffices with headroom
Both B and C represent valid counterexamples

questions.explanation: At small scale, vertical scaling can be more cost-effective due to lower operational overhead—no load balancers, no distributed coordination, simpler deployments, easier debugging. A $500/month large instance may cost less than three $200/month small instances plus the engineering time to manage them. Stack Overflow famously serves millions of users from a handful of powerful servers. Horizontal scaling becomes more economical at larger scales where hardware limits are reached and commodity hardware provides better price/performance ratios.

questions.question: A gaming company needs to scale their matchmaking service that maintains player state during matching. Which approach best balances scalability with state management?

options.text: Vertical scaling to keep all state in one process's memory
Horizontal scaling with sticky sessions based on player ID
Horizontal scaling with externalized state in a distributed cache
Event sourcing with state reconstruction on each request

questions.explanation: Externalizing state (to Redis, Memcached, etc.) allows true horizontal scaling without sticky session limitations. Riot Games uses this pattern for League of Legends matchmaking—player state lives in Redis, allowing any matchmaking server to handle any player. Sticky sessions create uneven load distribution and complicate failover. Vertical scaling has limits and creates SPOF. Event sourcing adds latency for state reconstruction. The fundamental principle: separate compute (stateless, horizontally scalable) from state (externalized, independently scalable).

questions.question: Which scenarios indicate that an application has reached the limits of vertical scaling? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: The largest available instance type is fully utilized
Adding more RAM no longer improves performance due to other bottlenecks
The application is I/O bound on a single disk or network interface
License costs for the software scale super-linearly with CPU cores

questions.explanation: Hardware limits (max instance size), diminishing returns (more RAM not helping because CPU or I/O is the bottleneck), and I/O bottlenecks on single resources all indicate vertical scaling limits. Oracle database licenses scaling with cores is a business/cost concern, not a technical scaling limit—you could still vertically scale if willing to pay. The technical limits are physical: there's a largest server you can buy, and single-resource bottlenecks (one NIC, one disk controller) can't be solved by making the server bigger. This is when horizontal scaling becomes necessary, not optional.
